source.title: A Theory of Generalization in Deep Learning

record.tranche_reason: The study derives a double-descent risk curve for a predictive-rank capacity path and reports an empirical comparison with that theory in a frozen-kernel setting. This is a different method and capacity measure from the original model-size sweeps.
record.gate_note: The study discusses double descent in its theory and reports a risk-versus-predictive-rank result in Figure 7. Its training-time grokking and overfitting results do not report the claimed fall-rise-fall epoch-wise shape. The noise and regularization discussions do not test whether those factors create, split, or remove a double-descent peak.
record.test_reason: In a frozen-kernel squared-loss setting, the study derives the risk along a predictive-rank path (Corollary H.3, Remark H.5) and shows empirical test risk matching it, with a double-descent peak (Figure 7A–B). This is a different method and capacity axis from the originals' model-size sweeps.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors present double descent as the rank-truncation instance of a unified frozen-kernel bias–variance decomposition. Along the predictive-rank path, adding a mode raises risk iff its noise exceeds its signal. They state the empirical risk matches theory 'without approximations' and that the peak sits exactly where the increment crosses zero.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a frozen-kernel spectral-filter and predictive-rank analysis rather than the original empirical sweeps over model size, training time, or sample size.
record.method_sensitivity: Along the predictive-rank path, whether risk rises or falls depends on the signal-versus-noise contribution of the added mode.

fits_no_version.finding: Under pure-noise interpolation, test error scales linearly with σξ² tr(Γ0) (Figure 7C).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Interpolation variance in the frozen-kernel limit equals the noise variance times the trace of the test-visibility Gramian (benign overfitting).

record.problems: The empirical capacity-axis result is presented in a figure without numerical values or model and dataset details in the text. The reported sweep uses predictive rank in a frozen-kernel setting and does not establish the result empirically across model classes.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results bearing on a tested version were omitted. Figure 7C's pure-noise scaling result does not test the claimed peak dependence on noise.

untested.parts: Comparison across several model classes; capacity measured as model size or parameter count; a peak at the training-set interpolation threshold. Only one frozen-kernel setting and a predictive-rank axis are shown.

Empirical multiple peaks (the theory allows several sign changes, but none are shown); removal of the peak under optimally tuned regularization (ridge is discussed in Proposition H.9 without a peak result); varying the label-noise level.
Figure 8 shows grokking and implicit bias over time, not an epoch-wise fall-rise-fall in test error.
No single complexity measure tested across axes.
No re-plotting against an effective parameter count.

missing.what: Model, data, noise level and numeric risk values for the Figure 7 empirical scatter; none are stated in the text.

record.verdict_notes: This is mainly a theory paper. The double-descent evidence is one figure with no reported setup details. The predictive-rank path orders modes by test visibility, so the shape depends on per-mode signal-to-noise along that ordering. It is not a capacity sweep past interpolation in the usual sense, so it bears on V4 only loosely. The deep-network results (grokking, PINN, DPO, INR) concern the authors' optimizer and do not bear on any version.

versions.untested_parts: No deep-network model-size sweep locating a peak near the training-set interpolation threshold.
No test-error fall-rise-fall sweep over training epochs.
No sweep over training-sample size near an interpolation threshold.
The reported capacity-axis result is for a predictive-rank path in the frozen-kernel setting, not an empirical comparison across multiple model classes.
No test of whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and sample size.
No test of whether noise or variance drives the peak, whether peaks split, or whether optimal regularization removes the peak.
No comparison showing that measuring complexity by an effective parameter count turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: frozen-kernel setting
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate test risk along a predictive-rank path.
rows.value: figure only; the caption says the empirical test risk aligns with the theoretical risk and shows a double-descent peak.
rows.note: The figure caption describes an empirical risk curve against predictive rank; no numerical curve values or model details are given in the text.
rows.check: The capacity axis is predictive rank: truncation to the top-r eigenmodes of the test-visibility Gramian Γ0, ordered by λj. It is not parameter count or model size. Full interpolation is reached only at r=ρ, so the 'interpolation peak' is an interior rank, not the training-set interpolation threshold. No dataset, model or numbers are given.

rows.subject: frozen-kernel setting
rows.operation_detail: Derive and examine consecutive risk increments along predictive rank.
rows.value: The increment is negative when the added mode's signal exceeds its noise and positive when noise exceeds signal; the text says the peak occurs where the increment crosses below zero.
rows.note: This is the study's theoretical characterization of the double-descent curve along the predictive-rank path.
rows.check: Mostly a theoretical identity (Corollary H.3), with an empirical increment curve in Figure 7B. It also bears on V6: per Remark H.5, the risk rises exactly when the added mode's noise exceeds its signal, a noise/variance-driven account of the peak.
